messages.subject: Re: Stacked Bar Graph Help
parts:
Hi:

This gives you the bar plot you described; your homework (and the prior probability this is a homework problem is pretty high) is to figure out *why* this works.

DF <- data.frame(class = factor(rep(c("Critical", "Error", "Warning", "Review"),
                                       each = 5)),
                  group = LETTERS[1:5],
                  count = c(1412, 45, 86, 381, 8, 475, 49, 12, 140, 172,
                            4, 2, 1, 4, 20, 125, 58, 17, 3, 117))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = group, y = count, fill = class)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
    labs(y = "Proportion", fill = "Class")


A few points:

1. I'm not convinced you understood the data structure you require for this plot, so I did that for you. In the future, instead of posting a screenshot of an Excel spreadsheet, it is courteous to have at least entered the data into R so that others can copy and paste it into their own R sessions. This does *not* mean copying and pasting data from the R console - the preferred way is to either supply the code that directly generates the data, as I did above, or to copy and paste the output from the dput() function, which provides the exact structure of your R object in text form. In this case, here is how you would do it:

dput(DF)

The output from this command should be copied and pasted into your e-mail:

structure(list(class = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 
2L, 2L, 2L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L), .Label = c("Critical", 
"Error", "Review", "Warning"), class = "factor"), Group = structure(c(1L, 
2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 1L, 2L, 
3L, 4L, 5L), class = "factor", .Label = c("A", "B", "C", "D", 
"E")), count = c(1412, 45, 86, 381, 8, 475, 49, 12, 140, 172, 
4, 2, 1, 4, 20, 125, 58, 17, 3, 117)), .Names = c("class", "Group", 
"count"), row.names = c(NA, -20L), class = "data.frame")

2. Like R-help, this is not a homework help list, although people here are less testy in their replies than on R-help. I would strongly encourage you to read through the Introduction to R manual and run the code on your machine. There are also a large number of R tutorials and several ggplot2 tutorials that can be found with a Google search. Learning from them will give you a better base from which to pose future questions.

3. The following link provides excellent advice about how to formulate questions to send to any R-related help list:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5963269/how-to-make-a-great-r-reproducible-example

4. At present, there is no 'official' ggplot2 tutorial, but there is an on-line set of help pages with numerous illustrative examples:
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/  This is often a good place to go if you want to create a ggplot2 graph with certain characteristics (although there is no example for this particular case on the geom_bar help page - I just checked).

The reason for mentioning all of this is because the better formulated your questions are, the easier it will be for others to provide potential solutions.

Dennis
